content_html:
Why Properties Matter

Every engineering component is made from a material chosen for a reason. A car crankshaft must resist repeated bending without snapping. A drinks can must be pressed into shape without cracking. A cutting tool must scratch other metals without wearing away. None of these applications can be designed without first understanding the mechanical properties of the materials involved. Choosing the wrong property match is one of the most common and costly errors in engineering design.

Key Fact

The seven mechanical properties you must know are: strength, stiffness, toughness, hardness, ductility, malleability and brittleness. Each describes a different response to mechanical force — and the same material can score highly on some and poorly on others.

Strength and Stiffness

Strength is the ability to bear a load without permanently deforming or fracturing. It is not one single thing — a material can have high compressive strength (resist squashing) but low tensile strength (resist pulling), or vice versa. Mild steel, for example, has excellent tensile strength, which is why it is used for structural beams that must carry suspended loads.

Stiffness is related but different. A stiff material resists deflection — it does not bend much even under a large load. Steel and concrete are stiff. A rubber band has low stiffness: it stretches easily under a small force. For structures like bridge decks and machine frames, stiffness is often as important as strength because excessive deflection can cause misalignment and fatigue cracking even when the material has not yet yielded.

Toughness is the ability to absorb energy before fracturing. A tough material does not shatter suddenly — it deforms, warns of overload, and only breaks after absorbing a significant amount of energy. Mild steel and nylon are tough. Tough materials are used where impact loading is a risk, such as car body panels, helmets and hammer heads.

Brittleness is the opposite of toughness. A brittle material breaks suddenly with little or no warning deformation. Glass and cast iron are brittle. This is not always a disadvantage — cast iron is used for machine beds where vibration damping matters more than impact resistance — but brittle materials must never be used where sudden impact loads are expected. Engineers say a brittle failure is more dangerous than a ductile failure because there is no visible warning.

Ductility and Malleability

Ductility is the ability to be drawn into a long shape — typically a wire — without breaking. Copper is highly ductile, which is why it is drawn into electrical wiring. When you pull a ductile material in tension it necks down and stretches before breaking rather than snapping clean. The percentage elongation at fracture is the standard measure of ductility: copper at about 45%, aluminium at about 25%, glass at near 0%.

Malleability is closely related. A malleable material can be hammered or pressed into a new shape without cracking. Gold is extremely malleable — it can be beaten into sheets just micrometres thick. Aluminium and lead are also malleable. The key distinction: ductility involves stretching in one direction (wire-drawing); malleability involves compression in all directions (rolling and pressing). A material can be ductile and malleable, or one without the other.

Key Fact

Ductility = drawn into wire (copper electrical cables). Malleability = pressed or rolled into sheet (aluminium foil, gold leaf). Both require plastic deformation without fracturing, but they apply in different directions and manufacturing processes.

Hardness

Hardness is the resistance of a surface to being scratched, indented or worn away. The Brinell hardness test presses a hardened steel ball into the surface; the Vickers test uses a diamond pyramid. A smaller indentation means a harder material. High-carbon steel, once hardened and quenched, reaches a very high Brinell number and is used for cutting tools, drill bits and files. Hardness and toughness often trade off against each other: a very hard steel tool can shatter under impact even though it resists surface wear perfectly well.

Exam questions often describe a component and ask you to identify a suitable material or property. The trap is answering with a vague word like “strong” or “light.” Instead, always name the specific property AND link it to the application. For example: “The bracket needs to be tough so it can absorb repeated impacts without fracturing suddenly.” The property + the reason is the full answer.

Some useful pairings to memorise: brake discs — hardness (resists wear from pads); suspension springs — strength and stiffness (stores energy without permanent deformation); body panels — ductility and malleability (pressed to shape); tools — hardness; cables — ductility and tensile strength; safety helmets — toughness. In machining, a hard material is difficult to cut (longer machining time, more tool wear) whereas a tough, ductile material machines to a good finish but takes up significant chip-forming energy.

Ferrous and Non-Ferrous Metals

All metals used in engineering fall into one of two families. Ferrous metals contain iron. This includes all the steels and cast iron. Because they contain iron, most ferrous metals are magnetic and will corrode in moist air if left unprotected — a thin layer of rust forms on the surface and, unlike the oxide layer on aluminium, it does not protect the metal underneath. Non-ferrous metals do not contain iron. Examples include aluminium, copper, lead and zinc. They are generally corrosion-resistant and non-magnetic, making them valuable in electrical, marine and food-contact applications.

Key Fact

Ferrous metals contain iron and are mostly magnetic and corrosion-prone: cast iron, low carbon steel, high carbon steel, stainless steel. Non-ferrous metals contain no iron and are mostly corrosion-resistant and non-magnetic: aluminium, copper, lead, zinc.

Steels and the Role of Carbon

Steel is iron with a controlled amount of carbon added. Increasing the carbon content raises hardness and strength but reduces ductility and toughness. Low carbon steel (also called mild steel) contains around 0.1% to 0.3% carbon. It is tough, ductile and easy to form and weld, so it is the most widely used structural metal — think RSJ beams, car body panels and the bracket used to mount a gate post. Low carbon steel does not harden well through heat treatment, which means it cannot be used for cutting tools.

High carbon steel contains approximately 0.6% to 1.4% carbon. The extra carbon makes it much harder and it responds well to heat treatment (hardening and quenching), so it is used for springs, chisels, files, drill bits and cutting tools. The trade-off is reduced ductility and weldability — high carbon steel can crack if welded without careful preheat. Stainless steel is an alloy of iron, carbon and at least 10.5% chromium. The chromium forms a passive oxide layer that prevents corrosion, so stainless steel does not rust even in wet or acidic environments. It is used for surgical instruments, food-processing equipment and architectural cladding.

Cast iron contains 2% to 4% carbon — much more than any steel. This makes it very hard, but also brittle: it cannot be bent, drawn or welded without cracking. What it can do is pour beautifully into moulds, picking up fine surface detail, and it damps vibration extremely well. These properties make it ideal for machine beds (the heavy base of a lathe that must absorb machining vibrations), engine blocks and manhole covers. Cast iron has good compressive strength but poor tensile strength, so it must never be used in tension.

Non-Ferrous Metals in Engineering

Aluminium is the most widely used non-ferrous metal in engineering. It has a density of around 2.7 g/cm³ — roughly one third that of steel — giving an excellent strength-to-weight ratio. It is highly ductile, corrosion-resistant (a natural oxide layer forms on the surface) and a good electrical conductor. These properties make it the default choice for aircraft fuselage panels, vehicle wheels, drink cans and overhead power cables. Copper is an outstanding electrical and thermal conductor, highly ductile and corrosion-resistant. It is drawn into electrical wiring, shaped into heat-exchanger tubing and used in plumbing. Lead is very dense, soft, malleable and highly resistant to corrosion and radiation — used for X-ray shielding and roofing flashings. Zinc is used mainly for the galvanising of steel: a zinc coating corrodes preferentially, protecting the steel beneath.

Key Fact

Aluminium has roughly one-third the density of steel but retains good strength, corrosion resistance and ductility. This strength-to-weight ratio makes it essential wherever reducing mass is critical — aircraft, high-performance vehicles and bicycle frames.

Alloys and How They Change Properties

An alloy is formed by melting two or more elements together, usually to improve on the properties of the base metal alone. The additional atoms disrupt the regular crystal lattice of the metal, making it harder for dislocations (the defects that allow slip) to move — this is why alloys are almost always harder and stronger than the pure metals they are made from. Brass (copper + zinc) is harder than either copper or zinc alone, and easier to machine into precision components than pure copper. Bronze (copper + tin) is harder than copper and more resistant to wear, making it ideal for bearings, propellers and bushings. Brass is also corrosion-resistant and has a gold appearance, so it is used for plumbing fittings, musical instruments and decorative hardware.

Properties are not fixed at casting — they can be changed by working and heat treatment. Cold working (pressing, drawing or rolling at room temperature) distorts the crystal grains, introducing dislocations that tangle and block further movement. The result is a harder, stronger but less ductile metal. This is why cold-drawn steel rods are stronger than the equivalent hot-rolled material. If ductility needs to be restored, annealing (heating and slow cooling) recrystallises the grains and relieves the internal stresses.

For high carbon steel, hardening by quenching involves heating the steel above its critical temperature (typically above 723°C) and then plunging it into water or oil. The rapid cooling traps a hard, brittle crystal structure called martensite. Tempering follows: the steel is reheated to a lower temperature (150°C to 600°C) to allow some internal stress relief and recovery of toughness, at the cost of a small reduction in hardness. Reducing grain size also increases strength: finer grains mean more grain boundaries to impede dislocation movement.

Polymers: Two Fundamental Families

Polymers are large molecules built from repeating chemical units called monomers. In engineering they divide cleanly into two families based on how they behave when heated. Thermoplastics soften on heating and harden again on cooling — the long molecular chains can slide past one another when warm. This means they can be remelted and reshaped, which makes them recyclable and suitable for injection moulding, vacuum forming and extrusion. Thermosetting polymers (thermosets) form permanent cross-links between their molecular chains during curing. Once set, reheating does not soften them — it chars or burns them instead. This gives thermosets superior heat and chemical resistance, making them useful for electrical fittings, cookware handles and adhesives.

Key Fact

Thermoplastics: ABS, acrylic, nylon, polycarbonate, polystyrene. Thermosets: epoxy resin, polyester resin, melamine, polyurethane, vulcanised rubber. A critical exam trap: polypropylene is NOT on this specification — only polystyrene is listed as the named foam/rigid thermoplastic.

Named Thermoplastics and Their Uses

ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene) is tough, rigid and easily moulded into complex shapes. It is used for computer keyboard keys, printer housings, crash helmets and LEGO bricks. Acrylic (PMMA) is transparent, UV-stable and weather-resistant, with a glass-like clarity at half the density of glass. It is used for shop display units, rear light lenses and aircraft windows. Nylon is self-lubricating, tough and wear-resistant: ideal for gear wheels, bearings and cable-tie heads that must operate without added grease. Polycarbonate combines high impact resistance with transparency — it is used for safety visors, CD/DVD discs and bullet-resistant glazing. Polystyrene is rigid and a good thermal insulator in its expanded (foam) form; in its high-impact form it is used for food packaging trays, model kits and disposable cutlery.

Epoxy resin is a two-part adhesive and matrix material: once mixed and cured, it is strong, rigid and resistant to chemicals and moisture. It bonds metals, ceramics and composites. Polyester resin is the most common matrix for glass-reinforced plastic (GRP) boat hulls and automotive body kits — cheaper than epoxy but slightly less strong. Melamine is hard, heat-resistant and hygienic: used for kitchen worktops and children’s tableware. Polyurethane provides thermal insulation in rigid foam panels and is used as a coating resin. Vulcanised rubber is natural rubber with sulfur cross-links added: it is tough, elastic and resistant to wear — essential for vehicle tyres, seals and conveyor belts.

Composites: Matrix Plus Reinforcement

A composite consists of a reinforcing material embedded in a matrix. The matrix (usually a polymer resin) holds the fibres in position and transfers load; the reinforcement (fibres or particles) provides strength and stiffness. Neither component alone has the combined performance of the composite. The properties of a composite depend on: the type of reinforcement, the direction of the fibres, the volume fraction of fibres, and the type of matrix.

Glass-reinforced plastic (GRP) uses glass fibres in a polyester or epoxy matrix. It is lightweight, corrosion-resistant and relatively cheap: used for boat hulls, roof panels and sports car bodies. Carbon-fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) uses carbon fibres in an epoxy matrix. It is stiffer and stronger than GRP for the same weight — the Boeing 787 uses a CFRP fuselage and F1 cars use CFRP monocoque chassis because the material combines very high stiffness with very low density. Fibre direction matters critically: fibres aligned along the load direction give maximum strength in that direction but are weak across it. Woven fabrics or cross-ply laminates are used when loads come from multiple directions.

Key Fact

In a composite, strength and stiffness are controlled by the reinforcement, but the fibres must be oriented along the direction of the applied load. Fibres running across the load direction contribute almost nothing to that load. This is why CFRP components are carefully designed as multi-directional laminates.

Structural Timber, Board Products and Ceramics

Structural-grade timber is graded by strength and used where a lightweight, renewable structural material is needed. C16 and C24 are the most common grades (the number indicates characteristic bending strength in N/mm²). Timber is strong along the grain but weaker across it — this is why structural beams run lengthwise. Plywood is made from thin veneers glued with alternating grain directions. Cross-graining overcomes timber’s natural weakness across the grain: the result is a panel that is strong and stiff in both directions, resists splitting and is dimensionally stable. It is used for structural flooring, concrete formwork and furniture carcasses. MDF (medium density fibreboard) is made from fine wood fibres bonded with resin under heat and pressure. It has no grain direction, machines cleanly and takes paint well, but it is not moisture-resistant and swells if wetted. OSB (oriented strand board) uses strands of wood bonded at specific angles for high strength and is used for structural wall sheathing. Ceramics (including engineering ceramics such as aluminium oxide and silicon carbide) are extremely hard and wear-resistant but brittle, so they are used for cutting tool inserts and heat-resistant linings — not structural applications subject to impact.

Structural concrete is a composite of cement, aggregate (sand and gravel) and water. Concrete is very strong in compression but weak in tension. Reinforced concrete adds steel rebar in the tension zones: the concrete resists compression, the steel resists tension, and together they can carry bending loads that neither could handle alone. Prestressed concrete goes further: the steel is placed under tension before the concrete is cast, putting the concrete into permanent pre-compression so that it can resist higher tensile loads before cracking. HS2 tunnels and multi-storey car parks are typical applications.

lesson_title: Material Costs, Supply and Stock Forms
content_html:
Why Cost and Supply Shape Material Choice

Even when a material is technically perfect for an application, it may still be the wrong choice if it is too expensive, difficult to source or unavailable in the right form. An engineer must always balance performance against cost, lead time and how much waste will be produced during manufacture. Stock forms are the standard physical formats in which materials are sold: sheet, bar, rod, tube, angle section, channel, wire, powder and granule. Using a standard stock form avoids the cost of special-order processing and means material can be ordered quickly from a distributor.

Key Fact

Standard stock forms include: sheet (aluminium, mild steel), bar (square, rectangular, round — steel, brass), tube (circular, square — steel, aluminium), angle section (steel structural), rod, wire (copper, steel), granule and powder (plastics for injection moulding). Off-the-shelf standard sizes minimise lead times and reduce cost.

Factors That Determine Material Cost

Raw material cost is driven by several factors. The rarity or abundance of the ore or feedstock matters: aluminium is abundant but energy-intensive to refine, so it is more expensive per kilogram than mild steel. Copper is moderately scarce and copper prices fluctuate with global demand from the electrical and electronics industries. Gold and platinum are very expensive because of their rarity and the complexity of mining and refining. The degree of processing also increases cost: a sheet of aluminium that has already been rolled, heat-treated and precision-cut to tolerance costs more than the equivalent mass of aluminium ingot. Any material that has been pre-machined or treated will carry a premium over raw stock.

Economies of scale (also called bulk pricing or price breaks) mean that the unit cost of a material falls as the quantity ordered rises. A small workshop ordering 10 steel bars pays a higher price per bar than a large manufacturer ordering 10,000 bars of the same specification. This is because the supplier’s delivery, handling, warehousing and order-processing costs are spread across a larger number of units. Engineers ordering for a prototype batch need to be aware that their per-unit material cost will be much higher than the production-run cost, which affects how accurately they can predict the final product price.

Not all materials are equally available everywhere. Lead time is the delay between ordering and receiving a material. For standard stock held in a local distributor’s warehouse, lead time might be next-day delivery. For specialist alloys, custom-profile extrusions or material in unusual thicknesses, lead time can be weeks or months. Global supply chains mean that a political crisis, port disruption or natural disaster in a producing country can suddenly make a material unavailable or very expensive. Engineers are increasingly required to consider whether a second-choice material could be substituted if the primary supply chain was disrupted — this is called dual-sourcing or supply-chain resilience planning.

Comparing Material Costs: Three Examples

Understanding relative cost is as important as knowing absolute price. Consider these comparisons:

Copper vs gold for electrical contacts. Both are excellent conductors, but gold is roughly 60,000 times more expensive per kilogram than copper. Copper is used for all general-purpose electrical wiring and contacts. Gold is reserved only for high-reliability micro-contacts (spacecraft, medical implants) where its superior corrosion resistance justifies the premium cost and where the contact area is tiny so the total mass of gold is very small. For a consumer power cable, using gold would make the product impossibly expensive to market.

Timber vs structural steel for a roof beam. Structural timber (C24 grade) costs significantly less per metre of beam than an equivalent steel RSJ, and timber is a renewable resource. For a domestic roof span up to about 6 metres, timber is the standard choice. For longer spans or where fire resistance is critical, steel is preferred despite its higher cost, because its strength-to-cross-section ratio and non-combustibility justify the premium. The engineer must calculate whether the saving on material cost outweighs the higher fabrication cost of steel.

Polymer housing vs metal housing for a handheld tool. Injection-moulded nylon or ABS housing is far cheaper to produce in large quantities than an equivalent aluminium alloy die-casting: the tooling cost is similar, but the cycle time is shorter and no machining or surface treatment is needed. For small quantities (fewer than a few hundred units) machined aluminium may actually be cheaper because expensive injection-mould tooling cannot be amortised over enough units.

Key Fact

Economies of scale reduce unit cost as quantity rises because fixed costs (delivery, handling, tooling, setup) are spread over more parts. This is why prototype unit costs are always much higher than production-run unit costs — an important factor when giving clients a production-price estimate.

A common calculation question involves working out how many parts fit on a standard sheet and what the resulting material cost per part is. The critical trap is dividing sheet area by part area and treating the result as the number of parts. In practice, parts must be laid out in a rectangular grid (or an efficient nesting pattern) and you cannot use partial parts. The correct method is:

Step 1 — Divide the sheet length by the part length (round DOWN to the nearest whole number) to find how many fit along the length. Step 2 — Divide the sheet width by the part width (round DOWN) to find how many fit across the width. Step 3 — Multiply the two whole numbers to find total parts per sheet. Step 4 — Divide the sheet cost by the number of parts to find material cost per part. The waste (offcut) area is the difference between the sheet area and the total area of all the cut parts. Minimising this waste is a key goal of production planning — nesting software on CNC cutting machines optimises layouts automatically.

lesson_title: Factors Influencing Design: Energy, Lifespan and Maintenance
content_html:
Energy Sources in Engineering Context

Every product an engineer designs relies on energy somewhere in its life cycle — in manufacture, in operation, or in disposal. Understanding where that energy comes from and what its environmental consequences are is now a core engineering responsibility. Energy sources divide into renewable energy and non-renewable energy (fossil fuels and nuclear power, which relies on finite uranium reserves).

Key Fact

Renewable: wind, solar (photovoltaic and thermal), tidal, wave, hydroelectric, biomass. Non-renewable: coal, oil, natural gas (fossil fuels that release carbon dioxide when burned) and nuclear (produces radioactive waste, not greenhouse gases). The distinction between the specific environmental impacts of these groups is a key exam point.

Environmental Impacts: Specific Mechanisms

Vague answers like “bad for the environment” or “hurts wildlife” earn zero marks. You must name the specific mechanism:

Fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas): combustion releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that accumulates in the atmosphere and contributes to global warming and climate change. It also releases sulfur dioxide (acid rain) and particulate matter (respiratory health impacts). Extraction involves mining and drilling, which cause habitat loss and risk of oil spills. Nuclear: does not release greenhouse gases during operation, but produces high-level radioactive waste that must be stored securely for thousands of years. A reactor accident (such as Chernobyl or Fukushima) can contaminate large areas with long-lived radioactive isotopes. Wind: no greenhouse gas emissions during operation, but wind turbines cause noise, affect local visual landscape and can kill birds and bats if sited on migration routes. Offshore wind has a smaller land-use impact. Solar: no operational emissions, but manufacturing photovoltaic panels uses energy and toxic chemicals. Land-use for large solar farms can displace habitats. Tidal: predictable and reliable (unlike wind and solar), no emissions, but tidal barrages can affect estuarine ecosystems and sediment transport. Biomass: burning biomass releases carbon dioxide, but if the biomass is regrown, the carbon is re-absorbed over the growth cycle — making it roughly carbon-neutral, though transport emissions add to the total.

Engineered lifespan is the design decision to build a product to last for a defined period — long enough to be useful, but not necessarily forever. A domestic washing machine might be designed for a 10-year service life; a commercial aircraft for 25 years or a specific number of pressurisation cycles. Designing for a finite lifespan allows engineers to optimise material use and cost, because they do not need to over-engineer components beyond what the expected service conditions demand.

Planned obsolescence takes this further — it is the deliberate design of a product so that it becomes obsolete or fails within a predictable time, driving replacement sales. There are two forms: functional obsolescence (the product stops working after the designed lifespan, for example sealed batteries or glued components that cannot be replaced) and aesthetic obsolescence (the design is made to look dated quickly so customers choose to upgrade). Critics argue that planned obsolescence increases waste and resource consumption. The UK and EU “right to repair” legislation is introducing requirements for manufacturers to supply spare parts and allow user repair for an extended period.

Maintenance Requirements in Engineering Design

Some products are designed for easy maintenance; others are designed to be sealed for life. The choice affects material selection, fastener choice and the design of access points. The main maintenance activities an engineer must consider are:

Lubrication. Moving parts in contact generate friction and wear. Sealed bearings (such as those in a bicycle hub) contain grease for the life of the bearing. Industrial gearboxes have oil-fill ports and oil-change service intervals. Nylon and PTFE components are self-lubricating and require no external oil or grease. Avoiding corrosion. Steel components in outdoor or marine environments must be protected: galvanising (zinc coating), painting, anodising (aluminium), use of stainless steel or plastic enclosures. For a coastal wind turbine nacelle, corrosion protection adds significantly to whole-life cost if not designed in from the start. Compensating for wear. Brake pads, tyres and conveyor belts wear in service. Design must allow these to be measured (indicator grooves on brake pads, tread-depth indicators on tyres) and replaced without dismantling the entire assembly. A service interval defines how often a product must be inspected and consumable parts replaced.

Key Fact

The three engineering maintenance categories are: lubrication (sealed bearings, oil-change intervals, self-lubricating materials like nylon), corrosion avoidance (galvanising, painting, stainless steel, anodising) and wear compensation (measurable wear indicators, replaceable consumables, defined service intervals). All three should be built into a design from the start, not retrofitted.

At the end of a product’s service life, the engineer’s responsibilities do not stop. Recovery of materials (recycling) is increasingly a legal requirement and a commercial priority. Metals are the most efficiently recycled engineering materials: steel and aluminium scrap can be remelted and re-rolled into new stock with a fraction of the energy needed to produce primary metal from ore. Aluminium recycling uses only about 5% of the energy of primary smelting. Thermoplastics can be remelted and granulated for re-moulding, though multiple recycling cycles degrade polymer chains and reduce quality. Thermosets and composites are difficult to recycle because they cannot be remelted; they are typically shredded for use as filler material or incinerated for energy recovery. Designing for disassembly (using screws rather than glue, labelling polymer types with recycling codes) makes end-of-life recovery easier.

What Is Additive Manufacturing?

Additive manufacturing is the opposite of cutting or drilling: instead of removing material, you build a part up, one thin layer at a time. A digital 3D model (usually saved as an STL file) is sliced into hundreds of horizontal layers by software, and the machine deposits or fuses material along each slice until the full shape is complete. Because no specialist tooling — moulds, dies, jigs — is required, a new design can go from computer screen to physical object in hours rather than weeks.

Key Fact

Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer from a digital model (STL file). No moulds or dies are needed, so tooling cost is effectively zero for a one-off part.

Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM)

Fused deposition modelling (FDM) is the most common form of 3D printing found in schools and small workshops. A spool of thermoplastic filament — typically PLA or ABS — is fed into a heated nozzle. The nozzle melts the plastic and extrudes it in precise paths across the build platform. Each layer bonds to the one below as it cools, and the platform drops slightly before the next layer is deposited. A support structure is printed under overhanging sections and removed afterwards.

FDM is ideal for concept models, ergonomic prototypes and functional parts that do not need very smooth surfaces. Typical layer thickness is 0.1–0.3 mm. The main limitations are visible layer lines on the surface and relatively low mechanical strength compared with injection-moulded parts. Consumer FDM printers such as the Bambu Lab range have made this technology genuinely accessible at under £300.

Stereolithography (SLA) cures liquid photopolymer resin with an ultraviolet laser. The build platform starts just below the surface of the resin vat; the laser traces each layer, hardening only the areas it touches. The platform then drops by one layer thickness and the next cross-section is cured. SLA produces parts with an extremely smooth surface finish and fine detail, making it popular for jewellery, dental models and appearance prototypes in product design studios. Resin is more expensive than FDM filament and uncured resin requires careful handling as a chemical irritant.

Rapid prototyping using SLA is particularly valued when a design team needs a high-fidelity model to present to a client before committing to expensive injection-mould tooling. Dyson engineers, for example, use SLA models to evaluate cyclone geometry before the tooling investment is made.

Metal Sintering

Metal sintering (also called selective laser sintering or SLS when applied to metals, or DMLS — Direct Metal Laser Sintering) spreads a thin layer of metal powder across the build platform and a laser selectively fuses the particles. Unfused powder acts as its own support structure and is recycled after the build. The result is a fully dense metal component with mechanical properties close to those of a traditionally machined part.

Metal sintering is used across aerospace, automotive and medical engineering for parts that are geometrically too complex to machine conventionally — internal cooling channels inside a turbine blade, for instance, or a lightweight titanium bracket for an aircraft seat with internal lattice structures. Rolls-Royce uses metal sintering for low-volume turbine components. The process is slow and the machines cost hundreds of thousands of pounds, so it is reserved for high-value, low-volume parts.

Key Fact

FDM (thermoplastic filament), SLA (UV-cured resin) and metal sintering (laser-fused powder) are three distinct additive routes. FDM is cheapest; SLA gives the best surface finish; metal sintering produces functional metal parts with complex geometry.

Additive Manufacturing vs Mass Production

A common error is to describe additive manufacturing as a mass-production method. It is not. The table below captures the key differences examiners reward.

Tooling cost: Additive manufacturing requires no moulds, dies or fixtures — the digital model is sent straight to the machine. Injection moulding, by contrast, requires a steel mould that can cost £20,000–£200,000 before a single part is made. Additive manufacturing therefore has zero tooling cost, making one-off and low-volume production economically viable.

Speed of iteration: A designer can update a CAD model and have a revised prototype in hand within hours. With traditional tooling, modifying a mould takes days or weeks and costs thousands of pounds. This is why product development teams use additive manufacturing for rapid prototyping during the design iteration phase.

Geometric freedom: Additive processes can produce internal cavities, lattice structures and undercuts that are impossible or prohibitively expensive to machine. Conventional subtractive machining is limited by tool access; additive is limited only by the digital model.

Production volume: Additive manufacturing is slow per part. A single FDM print of a mobile phone case takes 2–4 hours. Injection moulding cycles in 30–60 seconds. For volumes above a few thousand units, injection moulding almost always has a lower unit cost once the tooling cost is amortised.

Material waste: Additive manufacturing adds material only where needed — waste is minimal. Subtractive processes (milling, turning) can waste 90% of the starting billet for complex aerospace parts. This makes additive manufacturing more sustainable for expensive materials such as titanium.

Rapid Prototyping in the Engineering Design Process

Rapid prototyping sits between the design phase and the production phase. An engineer creates a CAD model, exports it as an STL file, and feeds it to an additive manufacturing machine. The resulting prototype is used to test fit, form and function before committing to expensive tooling. This compresses the design cycle significantly: Tesla’s Gigafactory uses additive manufacturing to iterate on manufacturing jigs and tooling fixtures at speed, avoiding the lead times of conventional fabrication. Once the design is finalised, mass production typically uses a different process — injection moulding, die casting or CNC machining — better suited to high volumes.

lesson_title: Material Removal: Cutting, Turning, Milling, Drilling
content_html:
What Is Subtractive Manufacturing?

Subtractive manufacturing starts with a block, sheet or bar of material and removes unwanted sections until the finished part remains. Every process in this lesson — sawing, shearing, laser cutting, turning, milling and drilling — is subtractive. The removed material becomes waste (swarf, chips or offcuts), so material selection and planning the cutting sequence carefully both reduce cost and waste.

Cutting: Sawing, Shearing and Laser Cutting

The simplest subtractive operations separate a workpiece into pieces. Sawing uses a toothed blade — a hacksaw in the workshop or a band saw on the factory floor — to cut through metal, timber or plastics. The teeth are set (bent alternately left and right) so the kerf (slot) is slightly wider than the blade body, preventing binding.

Shearing uses two hardened blades (like giant scissors) to cut sheet metal without a kerf. A hydraulic guillotine can shear steel plate up to 10 mm thick cleanly and quickly. Because shearing requires no cutting fluid and produces no swarf, it is economical for straight-line cuts on sheet stock.

Laser cutting directs a high-power CO₂ or fibre laser beam onto the material surface. Controlled by CNC, it can cut intricate 2D profiles in metal, acrylic and timber with very narrow kerfs (as small as 0.1 mm) and no physical tool contact. Laser cutting is ideal for prototype sheet-metal brackets and signage panels but is limited to thin sections — typically below 25 mm for mild steel.

Key Fact

Sawing produces a kerf (slot) and swarf; shearing produces a clean cut with no kerf and no swarf; laser cutting produces a very narrow kerf and is CNC-controlled, allowing complex profiles to be cut automatically.

Turning on the Lathe

A lathe rotates the workpiece while a single-point cutting tool is fed along or into the material. Key parts of the lathe that examiners test regularly are:

  • Chuck — the rotating clamp at the headstock that grips the workpiece. A three-jaw self-centring chuck grips round or hexagonal bar automatically; a four-jaw independent chuck can grip irregular shapes.
  • Tailstock — the adjustable support at the opposite end of the bed. It can hold a live centre to support long workpieces, or a drill chuck for drilling on the lathe’s axis.
  • Carriage / tool post — holds the cutting tool and moves along the bed (for parallel turning) or across (for facing).
  • Bed — the precision-machined base that ensures the carriage moves parallel to the spindle axis.

Lathe operations include parallel (cylindrical) turning (reducing diameter along the length), facing (cutting across the end to produce a flat face), taper turning (angling the tool path to create a cone), and boring (enlarging an existing hole from the inside). Cutting speed and feed rate are set to suit the workpiece material — harder metals require slower speeds and a finer feed.

Every material has a recommended cutting speed (in metres per minute, m/min) — the speed at which the cutting tool moves through the material at the point of contact. For a rotating workpiece on a lathe, this depends on both the spindle speed (revolutions per minute, rpm) and the diameter of the workpiece.

The relationship is: $$N = \frac{1000 \times v}{\pi \times d}$$ where \(N\) = spindle speed (rpm), \(v\) = cutting speed (m/min), \(d\) = workpiece diameter (mm).

Worked example: A 40 mm diameter mild steel bar is to be turned. The recommended cutting speed for mild steel is 30 m/min. Find the required spindle speed. $$N = \frac{1000 \times 30}{\pi \times 40} = \frac{30\,000}{125.66} \approx 239 \text{ rpm}$$ The lathe would be set to the nearest available speed below 239 rpm to avoid over-speed and tool damage.

Notice that a larger diameter requires a lower spindle speed to maintain the same cutting speed at the surface. If the diameter halves, the spindle speed must double. This inverse relationship is a common exam question.

Milling

Milling uses a rotating multi-tooth cutter. Unlike a lathe (where the workpiece rotates), in milling the cutter rotates and the workpiece is clamped to a table that moves in X, Y and Z directions. Milling operations include:

  • Face milling — a large-diameter cutter with many teeth sweeps across the top surface to produce a flat, smooth face. Used to true-up castings and forgings.
  • Slot milling — an end mill (a cutter with teeth on its end and sides) cuts a slot or keyway into the workpiece surface.
  • Profile milling — the CNC table follows a programmed path to cut complex 2D or 3D shapes, used heavily in aerospace for aluminium wing ribs and in automotive for cylinder-head ports.
Key Fact

On a lathe the workpiece rotates and the tool is stationary (moves linearly). On a milling machine the cutter rotates and the workpiece is clamped to a moving table. Getting this the wrong way round is a common exam mistake.

Drilling

A pillar drill (also called a drill press) holds a drill bit in a rotating chuck and feeds it vertically into the workpiece. Tool names examiners expect you to know:

  • Centre drill — a short, rigid combined drill-and-countersink used first to create a precise starting point, preventing the twist drill from wandering.
  • Twist drill — the standard helical drill for producing through-holes and blind holes. Flutes carry swarf out of the hole.
  • Countersink — a conical cutter that bevels the top of a hole so a countersunk screw sits flush with the surface.
  • Counterbore — a stepped cutter that enlarges the top of a hole to receive a cap-head bolt so its head sits below the surface.

The sequence for drilling a precision hole is: mark out the centre with a centre punch → use a centre drill to start the hole accurately → drill the through-hole with a twist drill at the correct speed → de-burr the hole edges. Giving “drill” alone in an answer is not specific enough; always state the type of drill bit.

Chemical etching is used to produce printed circuit boards (PCBs). The process is subtractive but uses chemistry rather than mechanical cutting. A blank PCB consists of a fibreglass substrate coated in a thin copper layer. The desired circuit pattern is printed onto the copper using UV-sensitive etch-resist film, which is exposed and developed. The board is then immersed in ferric chloride (iron(III) chloride) solution, which dissolves the unprotected copper while leaving the resist-covered tracks intact. After etching, the resist is removed, revealing the finished copper tracks. Chemical etching bridges the Manufacturing and Systems units because PCBs are the foundation of electronic circuits.

Four Distinct Families

Shaping, casting and moulding all give material a new form without removing it as waste chips — but the mechanisms are completely different. A common exam error is mixing stages from different processes. Keep these four families separate from the start:

  • Press forming — squeeze a sheet between two solid dies to change its shape in the solid state.
  • Injection moulding — melt polymer granules and inject under pressure into a closed metal mould.
  • Sand casting — pour liquid metal into a cavity formed by compressing sand around a pattern.
  • Pressure die casting — inject liquid metal under high pressure into a precision reusable steel die.

Press Forming (and Related Sheet-Metal Operations)

Press forming places a flat sheet of metal between a punch (upper male tool) and a die (lower female tool). The press ram drives the punch down with enormous force — hundreds of tonnes for structural pressings — deforming the sheet permanently into the die cavity. The car body panel on every modern car is made this way: the outer skin of a vehicle door takes less than a second to press from a flat steel blank. Related sheet-metal operations include:

  • Bending and folding — a press-brake bends sheet along a straight line; a box-and-pan folder creates enclosure cases and duct sections.
  • Punching and blanking — a punch shears a hole (punching) or cuts a shaped blank (blanking) from sheet stock in a single stroke.
  • Stamping — a high-speed press stamps (embosses or cuts) repeated features — such as the tabs on a battery connector — into sheet at production rates of thousands per hour.
  • Composite lay-up — individual layers of glass-fibre or carbon-fibre cloth pre-impregnated with resin (“prepreg”) are laid by hand into a mould, then cured under heat and pressure in an autoclave. Used for F1 monocoques and wind-turbine blades where weight is critical.
Key Fact

Press forming acts on solid sheet metal between a punch and die. Vacuum forming stretches a heated thermoplastic sheet over a single mould using atmospheric pressure. Injection moulding melts polymer and injects it under pressure into a closed mould. These are three distinct processes — mixing their stages in an answer loses marks.

Sand Casting

Sand casting is one of the oldest manufacturing processes still used today. A replica of the desired part — the pattern — is placed inside a two-part wooden or metal moulding box (the cope and drag). Sand mixed with a bonding agent is rammed tightly around the pattern. The pattern is then removed, leaving a cavity. If the part requires an internal void (such as a pipe bore), a separate core of sand is placed inside the cavity. The two halves are clamped together.

Molten metal is poured in through the sprue (the vertical channel), flows along the runner (horizontal channel) and enters the mould cavity through the gate. A riser (also called a feeder) is an additional reservoir of molten metal that compensates for shrinkage as the casting cools. Once solidified and cooled, the sand is broken away and the casting is removed. A draft angle on the pattern walls is essential to release the pattern cleanly from the sand without crumbling the cavity walls. The casting is then fettled (excess metal from sprues and runners is cut away) and may be machined to final dimensions.

  1. Place the pattern in the drag (lower half of moulding box) and ram sand tightly around it.
  2. Fit the cope (upper half) and form the sprue and riser channels using pegs.
  3. Remove the pattern carefully, leaving the cavity. Place any sand cores required for internal features.
  4. Reassemble cope and drag; secure together.
  5. Pour molten metal (e.g. cast iron, aluminium alloy) through the sprue until metal appears at the riser.
  6. Allow to cool and solidify fully.
  7. Break away the sand mould; retrieve the casting. Cut off sprues, runners and risers. Fettle and finish.

Pressure Die Casting

Pressure die casting injects molten metal — typically aluminium, zinc or magnesium alloy — under high pressure (10–200 MPa) into a hardened steel die. The die is precision-machined and can be reused for tens of thousands of cycles. The high pressure forces metal into fine detail and thin sections that gravity alone cannot fill. The cooling rate is much faster than sand casting (the steel die conducts heat quickly), giving a finer grain structure and better mechanical properties.

Advantages over sand casting: better surface finish, tighter dimensional tolerance, faster cycle time (seconds per part vs minutes), reusable die. Limitations: the steel die costs tens of thousands of pounds to make, so die casting is only economical at high volumes. It is also limited to non-ferrous metals — the high melting point of steel would destroy a steel die. Gearbox housings, engine covers and tap bodies are typical die-cast products.

Injection Moulding

Injection moulding is the dominant process for producing plastic parts at high volume. Polymer granules are fed from a hopper into a heated barrel where a reciprocating screw melts and homogenises them. When sufficient melt has accumulated, the screw acts as a plunger, injecting the melt under high pressure through the gate into the closed mould cavity. The mould is water-cooled, so the part solidifies in seconds. The mould then opens and ejector pins push the part free. Cycle times are typically 15–60 seconds for most consumer products.

Critical design features for injection moulding: the mould must have a draft angle on all walls so the part releases cleanly; wall thickness should be uniform to avoid sink marks and warping; internal ribs increase stiffness without adding bulk. The mould tool costs £20,000–£200,000 but is amortised across millions of parts. This process produces everything from mobile phone cases to car dashboards.

Key Fact

Injection moulding and pressure die casting both use a reusable precision metal die/mould; sand casting uses a single-use sand mould that is destroyed each cycle. The reusable die gives better surface finish and tighter tolerances but requires high capital investment.

Press forming: solid sheet metal, punch-and-die, high volume, excellent for thin-wall structural shapes.

Sand casting: any metal incl. ferrous, low tooling cost, disposable mould, low-to-medium volume, rough surface finish requiring machining.

Pressure die casting: non-ferrous metals only, reusable steel die, high volume, fine detail, fast cycle, high tooling cost.

Injection moulding: thermoplastics, reusable steel mould, very high volume, fine detail, fast cycle, high tooling cost, draft angles essential.

Permanent and Temporary Joining

Engineering assemblies require parts to be joined. The choice of method depends on whether the joint needs to be dismantled later, the materials being joined, the load the joint must carry and the cost of the process. Joining methods divide into two families: permanent (riveting, soldering, brazing, welding — joint cannot be undone without damaging the parts) and temporary (threaded fastenings such as bolts and screws — joint can be taken apart and reassembled). Understanding this distinction, and the temperature and filler requirements of each thermal process, is the key to answering exam questions correctly.

Riveting

Rivets are used to permanently join two or more sheets of metal. Pop (blind) rivets are used where only one side of the joint is accessible — common in aircraft skins and bodywork. Solid rivets require access to both sides: a bucking bar supports the tail while a rivet gun deforms it into a second head.

The correct sequence for riveting is one of the most-tested topics in the examination. Many students omit the marking-out stage and go straight to drilling, which means they lose marks. The full sequence is:

  1. Mark out — use a scriber and rule to mark the rivet positions on the top sheet.
  2. Centre-punch each marked position to prevent the drill wandering.
  3. Clamp the sheets together in the correct position.
  4. Drill the rivet holes through both sheets using a twist drill of the correct diameter.
  5. De-burr the holes to remove sharp edges.
  6. Insert the rivet through the aligned holes.
  7. Form the tail — use a rivet snap (or for pop rivets, the rivet gun) to peen (deform) the tail into the second head, clamping the sheets together.
Key Fact

The riveting sequence always starts with marking out. Skipping this stage — going directly from “select rivet” to “drill” — is the single most common error on joining questions and costs marks every year.

Threaded Fastenings (Temporary Joining)

Bolts, machine screws and set screws are threaded fastenings. A bolt passes through clearance holes in both parts and is secured by a nut on the reverse; a machine screw threads into a tapped hole in one part. Threaded fastenings are temporary: they can be removed with a spanner or screwdriver, which makes them essential for assemblies that need maintenance access — such as engine covers, gearbox housings and electrical panels. Locking devices (spring washers, nyloc nuts, thread-locking adhesive) prevent vibration-induced loosening.

Soft Soldering

Soft soldering uses a filler metal with a melting point below 450 °C — traditionally a tin-lead alloy, now typically lead-free tin-copper or tin-silver for health reasons. The soldering iron heats the joint; flux is applied to remove oxide films and allow the solder to flow; the filler melts and fills the gap by capillary action. The parent metal does not melt. Soft solder is used for electronic circuit-board connections and for joining copper water pipes (plumbing). The joint is weaker than the parent metal and not suitable for structural applications.

Hard soldering (also called silver soldering) uses a filler alloy containing silver, with a melting point between 450 °C and 900 °C. The process is otherwise similar to soft soldering — the parent metal is not melted — but the joint is significantly stronger and more heat-resistant. Hard soldering is used to join copper and brass components in plumbing and jewellery.

Brazing uses a brass filler rod (typically 60% copper, 40% zinc) with a melting point around 870 °C to join steel or copper parts. A blowtorch or oxy-acetylene torch heats the joint area to the correct temperature (cherry-red for steel). Flux is applied to prevent oxidation. The filler rod is touched to the hot joint and melts into the gap by capillary action — the engineer must NOT melt the filler directly in the flame. The parent metal is not melted. This is the critical distinction: brazing uses a filler rod at a temperature below the parent metal’s melting point. Welding (below) melts the parent metal itself.

A common exam error is confusing soft soldering and brazing. The temperature is the key: soft solder < 450 °C; brazing > 450 °C (typically 870 °C for brass filler). Another error is confusing brazing with welding: in brazing, the parent metal remains solid; in welding, the parent metal melts.

Welding

Welding is the only joining process listed here in which the parent metal melts. An electric arc or oxy-acetylene flame generates temperatures above the melting point of the steel (above 1,500 °C), creating a molten pool at the joint. A filler rod (or the wire electrode in MIG welding) adds material to the pool, which solidifies into a continuous fusion bond on cooling.

Common welding processes:

  • MIG (Metal Inert Gas) welding — a continuously fed wire electrode melts into the joint, shielded by an inert gas (argon or CO₂) to exclude oxygen. MIG is fast, highly controllable and widely used in vehicle body repair and fabrication workshops. BAE Systems uses MIG welding for structural steel fabrication on ships and aircraft ground equipment.
  • Arc (manual metal arc) welding — a coated electrode is clamped into a holder; the arc between electrode and workpiece melts both the electrode coating (which provides a flux) and the parent metal. Slower than MIG but requires no gas supply, making it portable for site work.
Key Fact

Soft soldering < 450 °C, parent metal not melted. Brazing > 450 °C (brass filler rod), parent metal not melted. Welding: parent metal melts — this is what distinguishes it from all other thermal joining methods.

Soft soldering: temp < 450 °C | filler: tin alloy | parent metal: does NOT melt | materials: copper, steel, PCB | use: electronics, plumbing

Hard soldering / silver soldering: temp 450–900 °C | filler: silver alloy | parent metal: does NOT melt | materials: copper, brass | use: plumbing, jewellery

Brazing: temp ~870 °C | filler: brass rod | parent metal: does NOT melt | materials: steel, copper | use: pipework, bicycle frames, small engineering assemblies

Welding (MIG/arc): temp > 1500 °C | filler: electrode wire | parent metal: MELTS | materials: steel (MIG/arc), aluminium (MIG) | use: structures, vehicles, fabrication

Why Heat-Treat Metals?

The mechanical properties of a metal — its hardness, strength, ductility and toughness — are determined not only by its chemical composition but also by the size and arrangement of the crystals (grains) inside it. Heat treatment deliberately alters grain structure by controlling how a metal is heated and then cooled. This gives engineers the ability to adjust properties after manufacturing: soften a steel so it can be bent without cracking, or harden a cutting tool so it keeps its edge under use.

All heat-treatment processes for carbon steel share three stages: heat to a soaking temperature appropriate for the process; hold at that temperature long enough for heat to penetrate the section (soaking); then cool at a controlled rate. The soaking temperature and cooling rate together determine which process you are performing and what properties result.

Normalising

Normalising restores a uniform grain structure after a manufacturing process that has distorted it. Forging, rolling, welding and cold working all introduce internal stresses and can produce a coarse or non-uniform grain. Normalising heats the steel above its upper critical temperature (typically 830–900 °C for medium-carbon steels) and then allows it to cool in still air. The still-air cooling rate is moderate — faster than furnace cooling, slower than water quenching — producing a fine, uniform grain structure. The result is a steel with improved toughness and consistent mechanical properties throughout the section.

Key Fact

Four key processes, four distinct purposes: Normalise = restore uniform grain after work-hardening or welding. Anneal = fully soften for further cold working. Harden + quench = maximise hardness (but brittle). Temper = reduce brittleness after hardening. These must not be confused with one another.

Annealing

Annealing is the process of making a metal as soft and ductile as possible. The steel is heated to above its upper critical temperature (same range as normalising) and then cooled very slowly — typically inside the furnace with the power switched off, taking many hours. This slow cooling gives atoms time to arrange themselves into large, coarse grains with very few dislocations, maximising ductility and making the metal easy to cold-work (bend, draw or stamp) without cracking.

Process annealing (also called sub-critical annealing or “softening”) is a variant used between stages of wire drawing or sheet rolling: the steel is heated just below the critical temperature and cooled slowly. This relieves the work-hardening that accumulates with each cold-working pass, allowing further deformation without fracture.

Hardening

Hardening makes carbon steel as hard as possible — but at the cost of making it brittle. The steel is heated above its upper critical temperature until it forms a uniform austenite structure throughout. It is then quenched (plunged rapidly into water, oil or brine). The sudden cooling prevents the atoms from reorganising into the soft structure they would normally form; instead, a highly stressed, needle-like microstructure called martensite is trapped. Martensite is extremely hard (the hardest microstructure in steel) but also very brittle — a hardened steel file will shatter rather than bend.

The choice of quench medium affects the cooling rate: water quenches fastest (maximum hardness, maximum distortion risk); oil is slower (slightly lower hardness, less distortion); brine (salt water) quenches fastest of all. For high-alloy steels, even air quenching may be fast enough to achieve full hardness.

A fully hardened steel is too brittle for most engineering applications — it would crack under impact. Tempering is always carried out after hardening to reduce brittleness while retaining as much hardness as possible. The hardened steel is reheated to a temperature below the lower critical temperature (typically 150–600 °C), held for a set time, then cooled in air. The heat allows some of the trapped martensite to transform to a tougher structure, releasing internal stresses.

The higher the tempering temperature, the tougher (and softer) the result. Colours appearing on a polished steel surface during tempering indicate the temperature reached: straw (230 °C) for woodworking chisels; blue (300 °C) for springs and screwdrivers; dark blue for saws. This temper colour method is a traditional way for a blacksmith to judge the tempering temperature without a thermometer.

Case Hardening

Case hardening is used when an engineer needs a component with a hard, wear-resistant surface and a tough, ductile core that resists impact. Gear teeth and camshaft lobes are classic examples: the surface must resist wear, but the core must resist the bending forces that would shatter a fully hardened component. Low-carbon steel (which normally cannot be hardened by quenching because it lacks sufficient carbon) is packed in a carbon-rich compound and heated in a furnace. Carbon diffuses into the outer layer over hours, raising the carbon content of the case to levels that allow hardening. The component is then quenched, hardening the carbon-enriched case while leaving the core (still low carbon) tough and ductile.

Key Fact

Case hardening gives a hard surface (to resist wear and pitting from contact forces) and a tough core (to resist the bending loads without shattering). Full through-hardening would make the gear tooth too brittle to withstand bending — it would snap rather than deform.

Normalising: heat above critical temp → cool in still air → result: uniform fine grain, relieved stresses, moderate improvement in toughness.

Annealing: heat above critical temp → cool very slowly in furnace → result: maximum ductility, coarse grain, softened for further cold working.

Hardening: heat above critical temp → quench rapidly in water/oil → result: maximum hardness (martensite) but brittle.

Tempering: reheat hardened steel below critical temp → cool in air → result: reduced brittleness, some hardness sacrificed for toughness.

Case hardening: heat low-carbon steel in carbon-rich atmosphere → carbon diffuses into surface layer → quench → result: hard case + tough core.

Why Surface Finish Matters

A surface finish does two things simultaneously: it protects the base material from corrosion and it gives the product its appearance. Both matter commercially: a rusted chassis is structurally weakened, and an ugly surface finish damages a brand. Surface finishing is the last manufacturing stage before a product leaves the factory, so faults here affect every unit that ships. Understanding which finish suits which material, environment and cost envelope is a key engineering decision that examiners test every year.

Surface Preparation

Every surface finishing process begins with preparation. Paint, dip coatings and electroplating all bond poorly to a surface contaminated with grease, rust, mill scale or dust. Standard preparation steps are: degrease (solvent or alkali wash), abrade (grit-blast or sandpaper to provide a mechanical key), rinse and dry. Skipping preparation is the most common cause of coating failure in industry. A well-prepared surface can make a cheap paint finish outperform an expensive electroplated coating applied to a dirty surface.

Painting and Spray Painting

Painting applies a liquid coating to the surface that dries or cures to form a continuous protective film. Spray painting uses compressed air to atomise paint into a fine mist that settles evenly across the surface. It is used on vehicle bodywork, metal furniture, machinery guarding and architectural steelwork. Multiple thin coats are better than one thick coat, which sags and cures unevenly. High-volume industrial lines use electrostatic spray guns that charge the paint droplets so they are attracted to the earthed metal workpiece, reducing overspray waste.

Advantages of painting: wide colour choice; low cost for low-volume work; can be applied on-site to large structures (e.g. the Forth Road Bridge). Limitations: can chip or scratch to expose bare metal, allowing corrosion to undercut the surrounding paint (the most common failure mode); requires ventilation and personal protective equipment (PPE) due to solvent fumes.

Key Fact

Paint can chip or scratch to expose bare metal. Once bare metal is exposed, corrosion undercuts the surrounding coating from underneath, spreading the failure zone. Galvanising (zinc coating) sacrificially protects even when scratched because zinc is more electrochemically active than iron and corrodes preferentially.

Dip Coating

Dip coating (sometimes called plastisol dipping or powder dip coating) involves heating the cleaned metal component to around 200 °C and then dipping it into a fluidised bed of thermoplastic powder (typically PVC or polyethylene). The hot metal melts the powder particles that contact it, building up a thick, rubbery coating. The component is then cured in an oven. Dishwasher racks, tool handles, garden-chair frames and cycle-basket wire forms are typical applications: the thick thermoplastic coating gives grip, insulates electrically, resists knocks and provides complete waterproofing.

Advantages over spray paint: the coating is much thicker (typically 1–3 mm vs 50–150 μm for paint), more chemically resistant, and resistant to impact without chipping. Limitations: colour range is narrower than paint; the process requires heating the component, so large structures cannot be dip-coated easily; it is more expensive than painting per unit for large flat surfaces where thin coverage is acceptable.

Spray paint: solvent-based or water-based liquid; thin coat (50–150 μm); wide colour range; can chip; low cost; suitable for on-site and large structures.

Powder coating: thermosetting polymer powder applied by electrostatic gun and oven-cured; thin but very hard and scratch-resistant coat; good colour range; cannot be applied on-site; better than paint for chip resistance.

Dip coating: thermoplastic powder, component heated and dipped; very thick, tough, rubbery coat; limited colour range; good grip and electrical insulation; best for wire forms and handles.

For an extended-response evaluation question, linking the choice to specific properties (coating thickness, chip resistance, grip, cost) and a specific application always earns the most marks.

Electroplating

Electroplating uses electricity to deposit a thin, uniform layer of a metal onto the workpiece surface. The component to be plated is made the cathode (negative electrode) in an electrolytic cell; the plating metal (e.g. chromium, nickel, gold, copper, zinc) forms the anode (positive electrode). Current flows through the electrolyte solution, dissolving metal from the anode and depositing it on the cathode surface. Chromium plating on car bumpers and taps gives a mirror finish and excellent corrosion resistance. Gold plating on electrical contacts reduces contact resistance and prevents oxidation. Zinc electroplating (electrogalvanising) protects steel fasteners.

Advantages: very thin (1–50 μm), dimensionally precise coating that adds almost no thickness to machined surfaces; excellent surface finish and appearance; can deposit expensive metals (gold, platinum) very economically because the layer is so thin. Limitations: the plating bath and anodes must be managed carefully; wastewater from plating is chemically hazardous and requires specialist disposal; not suitable for complex internal cavities where current density is uneven.

Galvanising

Galvanising coats steel with a layer of zinc. The dominant method is hot-dip galvanising: clean, fluxed steel is submerged in a bath of molten zinc at approximately 450 °C. The zinc reacts with the steel to form a series of intermetallic alloy layers, bonded much more strongly than a paint film. Street furniture, motorway crash barriers, agricultural machinery and structural steelwork are galvanised as standard.

Galvanising has one property that paint lacks: sacrificial (cathodic) protection. Zinc is more electrochemically active than iron; if the zinc coating is scratched through to bare steel, the zinc around the scratch corrodes preferentially, protecting the exposed iron. The zinc “sacrifices itself” to protect the steel. Paint has no such mechanism — a scratch allows moisture to reach the steel and corrosion spreads under the coating.

Key Fact

Zinc is more electrochemically active than iron. When both are in contact with moisture, zinc corrodes preferentially (sacrificial protection), so even a scratch through the galvanised coating does not allow the underlying steel to rust. Paint has no electrochemical activity — a chip exposes bare steel directly to moisture.

Polishing and Anodising

Polishing removes surface roughness mechanically — using abrasive compounds, buffing wheels or electropolishing — to produce a reflective, smooth surface. It is used on cutlery, surgical instruments, jewellery and any part where appearance or hygiene demands a smooth surface (rough surfaces trap bacteria). Polishing alone does not protect against corrosion but prepares the surface for electroplating or lacquering.

Anodising is specific to aluminium. Aluminium naturally forms a thin oxide layer that protects it from further corrosion, but anodising deliberately thickens this oxide layer using electrolysis. The anodised surface is hard, scratch-resistant and porous: dye can be absorbed into the pores before sealing, giving a wide range of colours. Laptop casings, window frames, bicycle components and camera bodies are commonly anodised. Unlike paint or plating, the anodised layer is part of the aluminium itself and cannot peel.

Ask three questions to choose the right finish: 1. What material is the workpiece? (Aluminium → anodising is most appropriate. Steel → galvanising, electroplating, paint or dip coating all possible.) 2. What environment will it face? (Outdoor, wet, salt spray → galvanising; food contact → electropolished stainless; decorative indoor → electroplating or paint.) 3. What is the production volume? (High volume → galvanising or electroplating bath; low volume or on-site → spray paint; small components needing grip → dip coating.)

For a 6- or 8-mark extended response comparing two surface finishes, the examiner rewards “similarities and key differences” rather than isolated bullet points about each finish. Always name the application, the mechanism of corrosion protection, the process steps and one limitation before concluding which is better for the specific scenario.

lesson_title: Describing Systems: Block Diagrams, Schematics and Flowcharts
content_html:
Thinking in Systems

Every engineered product — from a car braking system to a factory conveyor — is a system. Engineers break complicated products down into smaller, manageable pieces so they can design, build and test each part separately. The three main tools for doing this are block diagrams, schematic drawings and flowcharts. Understanding when to use each one is essential.

Key Fact

The input–process–output (IPO) model is the foundation of all system design. Every system takes something in, does something to it, and produces a result. Identifying these three stages is the first step when analysing or designing any engineering system.

The Input–Process–Output Model

The input–process–output model (IPO) lets engineers describe any system with three boxes. In an electric kettle: the input is the mains electricity and cold water; the process is the heating element converting electrical energy to heat; the output is boiling water. In a car engine: the input is fuel and air; the process is combustion; the output is rotary motion at the crankshaft.

A system also has a system boundary — an imaginary line that separates what belongs to the system from the wider environment. Drawing the boundary forces the engineer to decide exactly what is and is not part of their design.

System Block Diagrams

A system block diagram uses rectangular blocks joined by arrows to show how sub-systems connect. Each block is labelled with what it does (e.g. “temperature sensor”, “microcontroller”, “motor driver”). The arrows show the direction of signal or energy flow.

Block diagrams are NOT circuit diagrams and NOT flowcharts. A circuit diagram shows how components are wired using standard symbols (resistor, capacitor, LED). A flowchart shows the sequence of steps a process or program follows. The examiner has repeatedly noted that students draw circuit diagrams when asked for block diagrams — these answers score zero.

Key Fact

A system block diagram uses labelled rectangles and arrows only — no component symbols (resistor zigzag, capacitor plates, logic gate shapes). If the diagram looks like a circuit, it is wrong. Blocks describe WHAT each sub-system does, not HOW it is built.

Open-Loop and Closed-Loop Control

In an open-loop system the output has no effect on the process. A toaster set to a timer is open-loop: it heats for a fixed time regardless of whether the toast is burnt or pale. In a closed-loop system a sensor monitors the output and feeds information back to the controller. An oven thermostat is closed-loop: it measures actual temperature and switches the heating element on or off to match the set point.

Closed-loop systems are more accurate but more complex to design. Most industrial control systems — from a car cruise-control to a furnace temperature controller — are closed-loop because small disturbances (draughts, varying load) would cause the output to drift without feedback correction.

Large systems are broken into sub-systems. A car has sub-systems for engine management, braking, steering, lighting, infotainment and climate control. Each sub-system can be designed and tested independently. On a block diagram, sub-systems are shown as blocks that can themselves be expanded into more detailed block diagrams — this is called hierarchical decomposition.

The system boundary decides what counts as an input and what counts as an output. For a car engine management sub-system, “throttle position” is an input (from outside the sub-system, controlled by the driver), whereas “fuel injector pulse width” is an output (leaving the sub-system to control the fuel delivery).

Schematic Drawings

A schematic drawing (or schematic) uses standard symbols to show how components connect, not how they are physically arranged on a PCB or in a machine. Electrical schematics use British Standard (BS 3939) symbols: zigzag for a resistor, two parallel lines for a capacitor, a circle with an arrow for a motor. Hydraulic and pneumatic schematics use ISO 1219 symbols: rectangles for cylinders, diamonds for filters, arrows on lines for flow direction.

Schematics are the standard language of engineering workshops. If you hand a schematic to a technician, they can identify every component and trace every connection regardless of what the physical product looks like. This is why drawing interpretation is a key skill examined in the written paper.

Flowcharts show the sequence of steps in a process or control program. There are four standard symbols you must know:

  • Terminator (oval) — marks the START or END of the process. Every flowchart must begin and end with a terminator.
  • Process box (rectangle) — shows an action to be carried out, e.g. “Switch motor ON” or “Heat element for 30 s”.
  • Input/Output parallelogram — shows data entering or leaving the system, e.g. “Read sensor value” or “Display temperature”.
  • Decision diamond — asks a YES/NO question, e.g. “Is temperature > 80°C?” with two arrow paths leaving it.

Feedback loops in flowcharts must loop back to a decision diamond or an earlier process box — never to the start terminator. A common error is drawing the feedback arrow going all the way back to START, creating an infinite loop with no way to exit.

Choosing the Right Representation

The examiner expects you to choose the correct type of diagram for the question. Use a block diagram when asked to show how sub-systems relate and where signals flow. Use a schematic when asked to show component connections using standard symbols. Use a flowchart when asked to show the sequence of steps or decisions in a process or control program. Mixing these up is one of the most common reasons students lose marks on systems questions.

lesson_title: Mechanical Systems: Motion, Linkages and Cams
content_html:
Four Types of Motion

Mechanical systems transmit and transform movement. Before designing a mechanism you must identify what type of motion is needed at the output. There are four types that engineers work with every day.

Rotary motion is spinning around a fixed axis — a motor shaft, a gear, a wheel. Linear motion is movement in a straight line, such as the travel of a drill bit moving into a workpiece. Reciprocating motion is back-and-forth movement along a straight line — a piston, a saw blade or a needle in an industrial sewing machine. Oscillating motion is a swinging or rocking motion around a fixed point, like a pendulum or a windscreen wiper arm.

In the examination you must use the correct technical terms — answers like “goes round and round” or “goes sideways” are not credited. A motor produces rotary motion; a piston produces reciprocating motion.

Key Fact

The four types of motion are rotary (spinning around an axis), linear (straight line), reciprocating (back-and-forth straight line) and oscillating (swinging around a fixed point). Most mechanisms convert one type of motion into another.

Linkages and Conversion of Motion

A linkage is a set of rigid bars joined by pivots that transmits or changes the direction of movement. Engineers use linkages when they need to transmit force around corners, reverse direction, or change the shape of a motion path.

The simplest linkage is a reverse linkage (bell crank). Pushing one arm down causes the other arm to push outward — the motion direction changes by 90°. Bicycle brake levers use this principle: squeezing the handle pulls a cable that pushes brake pads against the wheel rim. A parallel linkage keeps two bars moving in the same direction — used in toy train pantographs and car suspension systems.

The crank and slider mechanism is the fundamental converter of rotary motion into reciprocating motion. A rotating crank pin is connected to a slider (piston) by a connecting rod. As the crank rotates, the slider moves back and forth. Every internal combustion engine uses this principle — the rotating crankshaft drives the pistons up and down.

The reverse is also possible: a reciprocating steam engine drives a piston back and forth, which turns a crankshaft via a connecting rod to produce rotary motion at the wheels. Engineers describe this as converting reciprocating to rotary motion.

Cams and Followers

A cam is a specially shaped piece that rotates and pushes a component called a follower up and down as it turns. The key principle: the position of the follower at any instant depends entirely on the radius of the cam at the point of contact. Where the cam radius is large, the follower is pushed up. Where the radius is small, the follower drops down. This is the examiner’s most-tested cam concept — you must be able to explain it, not just name it.

Key Fact

The follower’s position at any moment is determined by the cam profile — specifically the radius of the cam at the point of contact. A large radius pushes the follower high; a small radius lets it drop. The cam profile is therefore what engineers adjust to control the follower’s movement pattern.

Four cam profiles appear in engineering exam questions:

  • Pear cam — egg-shaped profile. The follower rises slowly to a maximum height and then drops quickly. Used in car engine valve timing, where a valve must open slowly and snap shut.
  • Eccentric (circular) cam — a circular disc with the pivot offset from the centre. As it rotates the follower rises and falls smoothly in a simple harmonic pattern. Used in pumps and simple oscillating machines.
  • Snail (drop) cam — the follower rises very gradually around most of the rotation, then drops almost vertically as it reaches the “snail’s tail” drop. Used in clock escapements and stamping machines where a sudden downward force is needed.
  • Heart cam — heart-shaped profile that converts the continuous rotation into a back-and-forth motion of equal rate in both directions. Used in mechanisms where a constant-rate reciprocation is needed.

Choosing the Right Mechanism

When an engineer needs to convert motion, they select the mechanism based on the motion required and the forces involved. To convert rotary to reciprocating: use a cam or a crank and slider.
